hints: Look closely at the puzzle: a measles vaccine is protecting against completely different pathogens, so ask yourself what the measles antibodies and those other pathogens must have in common.

Recall that antibodies are highly specific, but they can cross-react if shapes are very similar, and remember the difference between active immunity with memory cells and passive immunity with no memory.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Real Mystery**

Vaccination is artificial active immunity, so it makes memory cells. The mystery here is why measles memory helps against other infections when there is no measles around.

Think: the immune response must be recognising something shared.

**Apply Antibody Specificity**

Antibodies do not bind to just any antigen. Each antibody has a specific binding site with a complementary shape to its antigen.

However, if another pathogen has an antigen with a very similar shape to a measles antigen, the same antibody can bind to it. This is called cross-reactivity.

**Check Immunity Vocabulary**

Memory cells always mean active immunity, not passive immunity. And immunity from a vaccine is always artificial, not natural.

So we need an option that says: memory to plasma cells to specific antibodies that work because other antigens closely resemble measles antigens. That is option B.

options.A: Memory cells give active immunity, not passive immunity. Passive immunity involves ready-made antibodies with no memory cells involved.
options.B: This describes cross-reactivity. Anti-measles antibodies can bind to other pathogens if their antigens closely resemble measles antigens, giving extra protection.
options.C: Antibodies are specific and cannot bind to any antigen. They only bind to complementary antigens or very closely similar ones.
options.D: Immunity from a vaccine is artificial active immunity, not natural immunity. Natural immunity only follows actual infection, not vaccination.
